Task: Produce: (1) findings by category - what the documents show, with the document reference; (2) for each material finding: the issue, the risk and potential deal impact (price, indemnity, condition, walk-away), and the severity; (3) change-of-control, consent, termination and assignment issues triggered by the transaction; (4) gaps - expected documents not provided; (5) a prioritised Q&A list for the target and disclosure-schedule points.

Constraints: Report only what the provided documents show; do not infer facts or opine on the merits of litigation. Reference documents by index number. Distinguish confirmed issues from items needing clarification. Not legal advice - for the deal team and supervising partner.

Examples: Finding row: 'Material contract [Doc 4.2] - customer accounting for [X]% of revenue; change-of-control termination right on 30 days' notice. Impact: revenue at risk post-close; seek consent as a condition or price adjustment. Severity: high.'

Format: Sections: Findings by category | Material findings (table) | Change-of-control / consents | Document gaps | Q&A list for target. ~800 words.

Verification: Check every finding cites a provided document and every change-of-control trigger is supported by an actual clause; list documents in the index not yet reviewed.

Validation: The supervising partner must review before the report goes to the client. Pressure-test the severity ratings against the deal concerns: are the top 3 flags really the ones that would change the deal?

title: Write a board paper or governance briefing
description: A board paper with context, options, recommendation, and resolution wording.
prompt:
Role: Act as a company secretary drafting a paper for the board or a board committee.

Context: Committee / board and meeting date: [BODY_DATE]. Matter and why it is on the agenda now: [MATTER]. Background and prior decisions: [BACKGROUND]. Options and analysis provided by management: [OPTIONS]. Legal, regulatory or governance considerations: [GOVERNANCE_POINTS]. Recommendation from management: [RECOMMENDATION]. Decision or approval sought: [DECISION_SOUGHT].

Task: Draft the paper: purpose; concise background; the options with pros, cons and key risks; the recommendation and why; the legal/regulatory/governance considerations and any conflicts to note; financial and resource implications; and the specific resolution or decision the board is asked to make. Keep it tight and decision-focused.

Format: A board paper with numbered sections and a clear 'Decision sought' box. ~600 words plus any resolution wording.

Verification: Ensure the recommendation follows from the analysis and that all governance/conflict points raised in the inputs are addressed; flag anything needing legal review before circulation.

Validation: Read as a non-executive director seeing this cold: is there enough to decide, and is the ask unambiguous? Add or cut to make the decision clean.

title: Draft legal correspondence
description: Standard legal letters and responses in the right tone and structure.
prompt:
Role: Act as a paralegal drafting routine legal correspondence for a lawyer to review.

Context: Type of correspondence and recipient: [TYPE_RECIPIENT]. Purpose and the outcome we want: [PURPOSE_OUTCOME]. Key facts and dates: [FACTS]. Points that must be made: [MUST_MAKE]. Points to avoid conceding or stating: [AVOID]. Tone required: [TONE]. Deadline referenced: [DEADLINE].

Task: Draft the letter/email: appropriate opening, a clear statement of purpose, the facts and points in a logical order, the action requested and by when, and a professional close. Insert [PLACEHOLDER] for anything not supplied. Note where a lawyer must review before sending.

Format: A ready-to-review draft, followed by a short 'review flags' list.

title: Write a responsible-AI policy
description: Acceptable use, data handling, review requirements, and accountability for AI in your organization.
prompt:
Role: Act as a general counsel drafting a Responsible-AI use policy for the legal and compliance function.

Context: Tools in use or planned: [TOOLS]. Types of legal work AI might touch: [WORK_TYPES]. Confidentiality and privilege considerations: [CONFIDENTIALITY]. Client / regulator expectations: [EXTERNAL_EXPECTATIONS]. Data protection and records rules: [DATA_RULES]. Risk appetite: [RISK_APPETITE]. Applicable professional-conduct rules: [CONDUCT_RULES].

Goal: Give the team a clear, enforceable policy so AI improves legal work without risking privilege, confidentiality, accuracy or professional obligations.

Task: Draft the policy: (1) scope and definitions; (2) permitted uses (e.g. drafting aids, summarisation of provided material, research scaffolding) and prohibited uses (e.g. relying on AI-generated citations unverified, entering privileged or personal data into non-approved tools, delegating legal judgement); (3) mandatory human review gates and who signs off what; (4) data handling - what may be entered where, retention, and records; (5) accuracy and verification requirements (every citation and legal proposition checked); (6) disclosure expectations (internal and to clients/regulators where relevant); (7) accountability, training and breach reporting.

Constraints: The policy must not permit AI to be the basis of legal advice without qualified human review. It must protect privilege and confidentiality absolutely. Align with the professional-conduct rules provided. Keep it to a usable length (~900 words).

Examples: Rule shape: 'AI-assisted research: permitted for framing and locating issues; the lawyer must independently verify every authority and holding against a primary source before relying on it. Unverified AI citations must never appear in advice or filings.'

Format: A policy document with numbered clauses: Scope | Definitions | Permitted uses | Prohibited uses | Review gates | Data handling | Verification | Disclosure | Accountability & training | Breach reporting.

Verification: Check each prohibited use has a corresponding permitted-alternative or process, and that privilege/confidentiality is addressed for every tool named; flag gaps against the conduct rules.

Validation: Test the policy against three realistic scenarios (a rushed contract review, a research question, a summarisation of client documents): does it give a clear answer each time? Tighten any clause that leaves it ambiguous.

title: Implement a feature from a spec, with tests
description: Plans and writes production-quality code for a feature, including tests and edge cases.
prompt:
Role: Act as a senior software engineer working in an existing codebase.

Context: Feature spec / acceptance criteria: [SPEC]. Language, framework and versions: [STACK]. Relevant existing code / modules / patterns to match: [EXISTING_CODE]. Constraints (performance, compatibility, style guide): [CONSTRAINTS]. How tests are run here: [TEST_SETUP]. Non-goals: [NON_GOALS].

Task: Produce: (1) a short implementation plan - files to touch, the approach, and any interface changes; (2) the code, matching the surrounding style and patterns, with clear names and only the comments the codebase would use; (3) unit tests covering the acceptance criteria and the important edge cases; (4) a note on anything the spec leaves ambiguous.

Format: Sections: Plan | Code (by file) | Tests | Open questions. Code in fenced blocks with file paths.

Verification: State any assumption you made about the existing code you cannot see; do not invent APIs or config. Flag where the acceptance criteria are untestable as written.

Validation: Trace each acceptance criterion to a test; run the tests mentally against a tricky input and confirm the expected result. Note the riskiest part of the change.

title: Review my code for bugs, security, and quality
description: A thorough code review with prioritized findings and suggested fixes.
prompt:
Role: Act as a senior engineer doing a thorough but pragmatic code review.

Context: The code / diff under review: [CODE]. What it is meant to do: [INTENT]. Language, framework, conventions: [STACK_CONVENTIONS]. Known constraints and hot paths: [CONSTRAINTS]. Test coverage status: [TEST_STATUS].

Task: Produce: (1) correctness and safety issues (bugs, race conditions, error handling, security, resource leaks) - each with the location, why it is a problem, a failing scenario, and a fix; (2) clarity and maintainability suggestions ranked by value; (3) any missing tests; (4) what is good and should be kept. Keep opinions proportional - do not rewrite working code for taste.

Format: Sections: Correctness & safety (most severe first) | Maintainability | Missing tests | Keep. Reference code by file:line.

Verification: For each correctness issue give a concrete input/state that triggers it; if you are unsure it is a real bug, label it as a question, not a defect.

Validation: Re-check the top issue: would the failing scenario actually occur given the constraints and existing callers? Drop it if not, and say why.

title: Debug an error and find the root cause
description: Reproduces, isolates, and fixes a bug — with a test to prevent it coming back.
prompt:
Role: Act as a senior engineer methodically debugging a reported defect.

Context: Bug report (symptom, when it started, frequency): [BUG_REPORT]. Environment and version: [ENV_VERSION]. Relevant code paths, logs, stack traces, recent changes: [EVIDENCE]. What has been tried: [TRIED]. Constraints on the fix (compatibility, risk window): [CONSTRAINTS].

Goal: Get from symptom to a confirmed root cause and the smallest safe fix, with a test that would have caught it.

Task: Produce: (1) a hypothesis list ranked by likelihood, each with how to confirm or eliminate it from the evidence; (2) a reliable reproduction (steps or a failing test); (3) the root cause with the specific evidence that proves it (not just a plausible story); (4) the minimal fix and why it is minimal, plus any follow-up cleanup noted separately; (5) a regression test that fails before and passes after.

Constraints: Do not propose a fix before the root cause is evidenced. Prefer the smallest change that addresses the cause over a broad refactor. State clearly if the evidence provided is insufficient to confirm the cause and what to collect next.

Examples: Hypothesis row: 'H2: timezone handling in [function]. Confirm by: reproduce with a UTC-negative offset input; check [log field]. Eliminate if: the failure also occurs at UTC.'

Format: Sections: Hypotheses & how to test | Reproduction | Root cause + evidence | Minimal fix (+ deferred cleanup) | Regression test. Code in fenced blocks.

Verification: Explicitly separate what the evidence proves from what is inference; if the cause is not actually confirmable from the given evidence, say so and stop short of a fix.

Validation: Pressure-test the fix: does it address the cause rather than the symptom, and could it break an existing caller? Name the caller most at risk.

title: Write documentation, a README, or API docs
description: Generates clear technical documentation from your code or notes.
prompt:
Role: Act as an engineer writing clear developer documentation.

Context: The API / module (code or signatures): [CODE]. Who will use it and their level: [AUDIENCE]. Common tasks they need to accomplish: [COMMON_TASKS]. Conventions / doc style: [DOC_STYLE]. Things that trip people up: [GOTCHAS].

Task: Produce: a reference section (each endpoint/function: purpose, parameters with types and constraints, return value, errors, and one example); a short how-to guide covering the common tasks with runnable examples; and a 'gotchas' section. Keep it accurate to the code provided.

Format: Sections: Reference | How-to guide | Gotchas. Code and examples in fenced blocks.

title: Create a test plan and test cases
description: A risk-based test strategy with test cases for functional, integration, and end-to-end testing.
prompt:
Role: Act as a QA engineer designing tests for a new or changed feature.

Context: Feature and acceptance criteria: [FEATURE]. Architecture and integration points: [ARCHITECTURE]. Test framework and existing patterns: [TEST_FRAMEWORK]. Risk areas and past incidents in this area: [RISK_AREAS]. Data and environment available: [DATA_ENV]. Out-of-scope: [OUT_OF_SCOPE].

Task: Produce: (1) a test plan - scope, the risk assessment, the coverage matrix (scenario x test level: unit / integration / e2e), and entry/exit criteria; (2) detailed test cases for the highest-risk scenarios including boundary, negative, and failure-injection cases; (3) the automated tests for the unit and integration cases, in the project's framework and style.

Format: Sections: Test plan | Coverage matrix (table) | Test cases | Automated tests (code).

Verification: Map every acceptance criterion and known risk area to at least one case; flag scenarios that cannot be automated with the available data/environment.

Validation: Review coverage against the past incidents in this area: would these tests have caught them? Add cases for any that would have slipped through.

title: Triage defects and assess regression risk
description: Prioritizes bugs by severity and impact and flags regression risk.
prompt:
Role: Act as a QA engineer triaging defects and assessing release regression risk.

Context: Defect reports (symptom, area, frequency, environment): [DEFECTS]. Severity/priority definitions: [SEV_DEFS]. Planned release scope and changed areas: [RELEASE_SCOPE]. Test coverage by area: [COVERAGE]. Release date and constraints: [RELEASE_CONSTRAINTS].

Task: For each defect: assign severity and priority against the definitions with a one-line rationale, note likely affected users and any workaround, and flag if it is a regression. Then produce a regression-risk assessment for the release: which changed areas are risky given coverage and defect history, what additional testing is warranted, and a go / caution / no-go recommendation with conditions.

Format: Sections: Triaged defects (table) | Regression-risk assessment | Recommendation & conditions.

Verification: Apply the severity/priority definitions consistently; flag defects with insufficient detail to triage rather than guessing.

Validation: Challenge the recommendation as a release manager: is 'go' actually justified given the riskiest changed area's coverage? State the residual risk plainly.

title: Set up CI/CD and infrastructure as code
description: CI/CD pipelines and IaC templates with environments, checks, and rollback.
prompt:
Role: Act as a DevOps / SRE engineer provisioning a service the standard way.

Context: Service and its requirements (compute, storage, networking, scaling, availability): [REQUIREMENTS]. Cloud / platform and IaC tool: [PLATFORM_TOOL]. Existing modules / standards to reuse: [STANDARDS]. Security and compliance requirements (network, secrets, IAM, logging): [SECURITY_REQS]. Environments: [ENVIRONMENTS]. Deployment strategy: [DEPLOY_STRATEGY].

Task: Produce: (1) the IaC for the service using existing modules/standards where possible, parameterised per environment, with secrets and IAM handled per policy; (2) a CI/CD pipeline outline - stages, quality/security gates, approvals, deployment strategy, health checks, and rollback; (3) the observability wiring (metrics, logs, alerts) that should ship with it.

Format: Sections: IaC (code, per resource) | Pipeline outline (stages + gates) | Observability. Code in fenced blocks.

Verification: Do not hardcode secrets or account IDs - use variables/parameters and note where values come from. Flag anything that deviates from the stated standards or security requirements.

Validation: Walk a deploy and a failed deploy through the pipeline: does the rollback actually restore service, and do the gates catch a bad build? Fix the weak point.

title: Write an incident postmortem and runbook
description: A blameless postmortem with timeline, root cause, actions, and a runbook update.
prompt:
Role: Act as an SRE writing a blameless incident post-mortem and the follow-up runbook.

Context: Incident summary and impact (who/what, duration, severity): [INCIDENT]. Timeline notes and signals: [TIMELINE_NOTES]. What was done to mitigate and resolve: [ACTIONS_TAKEN]. Suspected causes and contributing factors: [SUSPECTED_CAUSES]. Monitoring/alerting state at the time: [MONITORING_STATE].

Task: Produce: (1) a factual timeline (detection, diagnosis, mitigation, resolution) with timestamps; (2) the root cause and contributing factors, written without blaming individuals - focus on systems, process and information gaps; (3) what went well; (4) corrective actions with owner, priority and due date, split into 'prevent recurrence' and 'reduce impact / detect faster'; (5) a runbook for handling this class of incident next time.

Format: Sections: Summary & impact | Timeline | Root cause & contributing factors | What went well | Corrective actions (table) | Runbook. ~700 words.

Verification: Separate timeline facts from reconstruction; flag any timeline gap and any cause not yet confirmed.

Validation: Review the actions as a sceptical engineering manager: would completing them actually prevent or shorten a repeat, or are they busywork? Strengthen the weakest.

title: Design a software architecture and weigh trade-offs
description: Architecture options, trade-offs, and a recommended design for a system.
prompt:
Role: Act as a solutions architect designing a system for a stated set of requirements.

Context: Problem and business goal: [PROBLEM_GOAL]. Functional requirements: [FUNCTIONAL]. Non-functional requirements (scale, latency, availability, cost, security, compliance): [NFRS]. Constraints (existing systems, team skills, timeline, budget, platform): [CONSTRAINTS]. Data characteristics: [DATA]. Assumptions and unknowns: [ASSUMPTIONS].

Goal: Give the team a clear recommended architecture and the reasoning, so the design decision is made deliberately against the requirements, not by default.

Task: Produce: (1) a context summary and the driving requirements; (2) 2-3 candidate approaches, each described at component level with how it meets the NFRs; (3) a trade-off analysis across the NFRs and constraints (a comparison table plus narrative on the key tensions - e.g. consistency vs availability, build vs buy); (4) a recommendation with the reasoning and what would change it; (5) key risks, spikes to de-risk them, and a rough phased delivery; (6) a text outline of the architecture diagram (components, responsibilities, data flows).

Constraints: Every option must be evaluated against the stated NFRs and constraints - no option dismissed on preference. Call out assumptions that materially affect the choice. Do not recommend a specific vendor product without noting the lock-in and alternatives. Keep it to ~1000 words plus tables.

Examples: Trade-off row: 'Approach | p99 latency | Availability | Ops burden | Cost | Time to first release | Main risk.' Tension note: 'Approach B gives strong consistency but caps write throughput at ~[X]; acceptable only if [assumption] holds.'

Format: Sections: Context & drivers | Options | Trade-off analysis (table + narrative) | Recommendation | Risks & spikes & phasing | Diagram outline.

Verification: List every assumption the recommendation depends on and mark which are unvalidated; flag any NFR that no option clearly satisfies.

Validation: Stress-test the recommendation at 10x the stated scale and against the tightest constraint: does it still hold? State where it breaks and the next design move.

title: Reduce cloud costs and right-size capacity
description: Finds waste and optimization opportunities in your cloud spend.
prompt:
Role: Act as a platform engineer reviewing cloud cost and capacity.

Context: Cost breakdown by service / team / environment: [COST_DATA]. Utilisation data (CPU, memory, storage, network) for the main workloads: [UTILISATION]. Commitments in place (reserved / savings plans): [COMMITMENTS]. Growth expectations: [GROWTH]. Reliability / performance constraints that limit changes: [CONSTRAINTS].

Task: Produce: (1) where cost concentrates and the trend; (2) waste - idle/underused resources, oversized instances, orphaned storage, inefficient data transfer, non-prod running out of hours; (3) right-sizing and architecture opportunities with estimated saving and the risk/effort of each; (4) commitment coverage recommendations given the growth expectation; (5) a phased plan starting with zero-risk changes, with a rollback note per change.

Format: Sections: Cost concentration | Waste findings (table) | Right-sizing opportunities (table: Change | Est. saving | Risk | Effort) | Commitment coverage | Phased plan. ~500 words.

Verification: Base every saving estimate on the utilisation data provided and state the assumption; flag changes that could affect the reliability/performance constraints.

Validation: Pressure-test the top 3 changes against a peak-load day: would right-sizing there cause a problem? Keep headroom and revise the estimate.

title: Write troubleshooting steps for a customer issue
description: Step-by-step troubleshooting guides for agents or customers, from simple fixes to escalation.
prompt:
Role: Act as an IT support lead designing assisted resolution for a request category.

Context: Request category: [CATEGORY] (e.g. VPN issues, access requests, laptop performance). Systems and knowledge sources of record: [SOURCES]. What the assistant is allowed to do vs must route: [BOUNDARIES]. Security rules (identity verification, least privilege): [SECURITY_RULES]. Escalation tiers: [ESCALATION]. Tone: [TONE].

Task: Produce: (1) an identity/eligibility check step; (2) a troubleshooting decision tree - questions, checks, and fixes in order of likelihood and safety, each citing the source; (3) the conditions that trigger escalation and to whom, with what context to pass; (4) the ticket notes template; (5) 3 example resolutions (a self-serve fix, a needs-approval case, an escalate case).

Format: Sections: Verification step | Decision tree | Escalation rules | Ticket notes template | 3 examples.

Verification: Ensure no step grants access or makes a change beyond the stated boundaries or least-privilege rules; every fix must cite a source. Flag any branch that could leave the user stuck.

Validation: Run a user who fails the first two fixes through the tree: do they reach a resolution or a clean handoff quickly? Shorten any path that loops.

title: Analyze security threats and vulnerabilities
description: Identifies vulnerabilities and threats and builds a prioritized remediation plan.
prompt:
Role: Act as a security engineer assessing security risk for a system or a set of findings.

Context: Scope (component, service, or finding list from a scan/pen test): [SCOPE]. Architecture, trust boundaries and data sensitivity: [ARCHITECTURE_DATA]. Existing controls: [CONTROLS]. Threat model context (who might attack, from where): [THREAT_CONTEXT]. Constraints on remediation (change windows, compatibility, resourcing): [CONSTRAINTS]. Framework / rating scale to use: [FRAMEWORK].

Goal: Give the team a clear, prioritised view of the real security risk and a remediation plan sequenced by risk reduction per unit of effort.

Task: Produce: (1) the threats / vulnerabilities identified, each with the affected asset, the attack path, exploitability, impact (confidentiality/integrity/availability and blast radius), and an overall rating on the given scale; (2) which are realistically exploitable given the existing controls and threat context vs theoretical; (3) a remediation plan - fix, mitigation, or accepted risk per item, with owner, effort, and the residual risk; (4) quick wins that reduce risk immediately; (5) detection/monitoring to add.

Constraints: Rate risk on the provided scale and justify each rating. Do not include exploit code or step-by-step attack instructions - describe the class of weakness and the fix. Distinguish confirmed issues from suspected. Respect the change constraints in sequencing.

Examples: Finding row: 'Asset: [service] API. Weakness: missing authz check on [endpoint]. Path: authenticated low-priv user calls it directly. Exploitability: high. Impact: read other tenants' data (confidentiality, cross-tenant). Rating: Critical. Fix: enforce tenant scoping in [layer]; owner [team]; effort M; residual: low.'

Format: Sections: Findings (table, ranked) | Realistic vs theoretical | Remediation plan (table) | Quick wins | Detection to add. ~700 words.

Verification: State the assumptions behind each exploitability rating and flag findings that need validation (e.g. confirm the control is actually absent) before remediation is scheduled.

Validation: Pressure-test the top finding as an attacker with only the stated access: does the attack path actually work end to end? If a control blocks it, re-rate and re-sequence.

title: Synthesize customer or user research
description: Turns interviews, notes, and observations into themes, insights, and opportunities.
prompt:
Role: Act as a product manager synthesising customer and market research.

Context: Research question / decision this informs: [RESEARCH_QUESTION]. Inputs provided (interview notes, survey results, support tickets, sales feedback, market data): [INPUTS]. Segments to distinguish: [SEGMENTS]. What we currently believe: [CURRENT_BELIEFS]. Constraints on what we can act on: [CONSTRAINTS].

Task: Produce: (1) 4-6 cross-cutting themes, each with the supporting evidence (which inputs, how many, representative quotes) and its strength; (2) where segments differ; (3) findings that contradict our current beliefs; (4) the 3 most decision-relevant insights and the product implication of each; (5) what we still do not know and how to find out.

Format: Sections: Themes (evidence-weighted) | Segment differences | Belief challenges | Decision-relevant insights & implications | Open questions. ~500 words.

Verification: Attribute every theme to specific inputs and note sample size; separate what the evidence shows from your interpretation. Do not generalise from one or two data points.

Validation: Test the top insight against a colleague who ran the interviews: does it match what they heard, or is it over-reaching? Adjust.

title: Write a product requirements document (PRD)
description: A PRD with problem, goals, users, requirements, scope, and success metrics.
prompt:
Role: Act as a product manager writing a PRD for engineering and design review.

Context: Problem and evidence it matters: [PROBLEM_EVIDENCE]. Target users and jobs to be done: [USERS_JTBD]. Proposed solution direction: [SOLUTION_DIRECTION]. Success metrics and current baseline: [METRICS_BASELINE]. Known constraints (technical, legal, timeline): [CONSTRAINTS]. Explicitly out of scope: [OUT_OF_SCOPE]. Dependencies: [DEPENDENCIES].

Task: Draft the PRD: problem statement and evidence; goals and success metrics (with targets); user stories / requirements grouped and prioritised (must / should / could); UX and edge-case considerations at a high level; scope and explicit non-goals; risks and mitigations; dependencies; open questions for the review.

Format: A PRD with numbered sections and a requirements table (ID | requirement | priority | rationale | acceptance idea). ~700 words.

Verification: Check every requirement traces to the problem or a metric; flag requirements that are really solution preferences without a why. Mark assumptions.

Validation: Review as a tech lead and a designer: is the problem clear enough to solve freely, and are the constraints and non-goals unambiguous? Tighten what would cause churn in the review.

title: Write user stories and acceptance criteria
description: Turns a feature into well-formed user stories with testable acceptance criteria.
prompt:
Role: Act as a product owner breaking a feature into backlog-ready stories.

Context: Feature and its goal: [FEATURE_GOAL]. Users and their context: [USERS]. Design or flow reference: [DESIGN_REF]. Technical notes / constraints: [TECH_NOTES]. Definition of ready and done: [DOR_DOD]. What is out of scope for this feature: [OUT_OF_SCOPE].

Task: Produce: a story map / breakdown into small vertical slices; each story in 'As a / I want / so that' form with acceptance criteria in Given/When/Then, the key edge and error cases, and any non-functional criteria; a note on stories that are too big and how to split them; and a suggested delivery order.

Format: Per story: Title | Story | Acceptance criteria (G/W/T) | Edge cases | Notes. Plus the delivery order.

Verification: Check each story against INVEST (especially independent and small); flag any acceptance criterion that is not objectively testable.

Validation: Have an engineer read two stories cold: could they estimate and build them without a meeting? Add detail where they could not.

title: Prioritize a product roadmap or backlog
description: Scores and orders features with a transparent model (RICE, value vs. effort) and builds a roadmap.
prompt:
Role: Act as a product manager prioritising the roadmap against strategy.

Context: Product strategy and current goals/OKRs: [STRATEGY_OKRS]. Candidate initiatives with what we know (problem, rough value, rough effort, dependencies, risks): [INITIATIVES]. Capacity available per period: [CAPACITY]. Fixed commitments / must-dos: [COMMITMENTS]. Stakeholders and their priorities: [STAKEHOLDERS]. Prioritisation approach preferred (e.g. RICE, weighted scoring): [METHOD].

Goal: Produce a roadmap that is clearly driven by strategy and capacity, with the reasoning visible so stakeholders can challenge the inputs, not the politics.

Task: Produce: (1) the scoring model - the factors, their weights, and how each is estimated, tuned to the strategy; (2) each initiative scored with the inputs shown and a confidence level; (3) a now / next / later roadmap that fits capacity and honours commitments, with the explicit trade-offs (what is NOT being done and why); (4) the initiatives whose ranking is most sensitive to a shaky input, and what to validate; (5) how to communicate it to stakeholders.

Constraints: Every score must use the stated inputs - do not invent value or effort numbers; mark low-confidence estimates. The roadmap must fit the stated capacity. Make the cost of the commitments/must-dos visible. No initiative ranked on stakeholder seniority.

Examples: Score row: 'Initiative | Reach | Impact | Confidence | Effort | Score | Notes'. Trade-off line: 'Choosing [A] over [B] this quarter costs us [expected value of B]; revisit if [condition].'

Format: Sections: Scoring model | Scored initiatives (table) | Roadmap (now/next/later) & trade-offs | Sensitivity & what to validate | Stakeholder comms. ~700 words.

Verification: Recheck each score against its inputs; list every initiative where a single uncertain input flips its position.

Validation: Pressure-test as a stakeholder whose priority did not make 'now': is the reasoning defensible on strategy and capacity grounds? Strengthen the explanation or revisit the call.

title: Map an opportunity solution tree
description: Connects an outcome to customer opportunities, solutions, and experiments.
prompt:
Role: Act as a product manager doing continuous discovery with an opportunity solution tree.

Context: Target outcome / metric to move: [OUTCOME_METRIC]. What we know about the current experience and its gaps (from research): [RESEARCH]. Constraints: [CONSTRAINTS]. Existing solution ideas on the table: [EXISTING_IDEAS]. Segments in focus: [SEGMENTS].

Task: Produce: the target outcome at the top; 4-6 distinct opportunities (unmet needs / pain points / desires) framed from the customer's perspective, each grounded in the research; a prioritisation of opportunities by impact on the outcome and how well-evidenced they are; 2-3 solution ideas per top opportunity; and, for the leading solution, the riskiest assumption and a small test to check it.

Format: A tree (outcome -> opportunities -> solutions), then: opportunity prioritisation | riskiest assumptions & tests.

Verification: Ensure opportunities are needs, not solutions in disguise, and each is tied to research evidence; flag any that are assumptions.

Validation: Check the top opportunity against the outcome: if we fully solved it, would the metric actually move? If not, reframe or re-prioritise.

title: Analyze my competitors
description: Competitor positioning, offers, strengths, weaknesses, and the gaps you can win.
prompt:
Role: Act as a product marketing manager benchmarking against key competitors.

Context: Our product and target segment: [PRODUCT_SEGMENT]. Competitors in scope: [COMPETITORS]. Buyer decision criteria and their weight: [DECISION_CRITERIA]. What we know about each competitor (features, pricing model, positioning, strengths, weaknesses): [COMPETITOR_INFO]. Evidence sources: [SOURCES]. Where we win / lose deals today: [WIN_LOSS].

Task: Produce: a benchmarking matrix (criteria x competitor, with a rating and a note); a positioning read - how each competitor is positioned and where the gaps in the market are; our genuine advantages and our real disadvantages on the criteria that carry weight; and 3 implications for product and 3 for messaging.

Format: Sections: Benchmarking matrix (table) | Positioning read | Our advantages / disadvantages | Implications (product / messaging). ~500 words.

Verification: Distinguish verified competitor facts from inference; do not overstate our advantages beyond the evidence or the win/loss data. Flag stale information.

Validation: Sanity-check the advantages against recent losses: if we are so strong on X, why did we lose deals where X mattered? Reconcile or soften the claim.

title: Plan user interviews or usability tests
description: A research plan with goals, participants, discussion guide, and tasks.
prompt:
Role: Act as a UX researcher planning a study.

Context: Decision the research must inform: [DECISION]. Research questions: [RESEARCH_QUESTIONS]. Study type (interviews / usability test / both) and setting: [STUDY_TYPE]. Target participants and where to find them: [PARTICIPANTS]. Prototype / product state: [ARTEFACT]. Timeline and number of sessions: [LOGISTICS]. Known biases to avoid: [BIAS_RISKS].

Task: Produce: sharpened research questions; a screener to recruit the right participants (with disqualifiers); a discussion guide (warm-up, background, core questions with non-leading phrasing and probes, wrap-up); for a usability test, 3-5 realistic task scenarios with success criteria and what to observe; a consent/recording note; and the analysis approach (how sessions will be coded and synthesised).

Format: Sections: Research questions | Screener | Discussion guide | Task scenarios (if applicable) | Consent note | Analysis approach.

Verification: Flag any question or task that is leading, double-barrelled, or primes the participant; check the screener actually excludes the wrong people.

Validation: Dry-run the guide against a likely participant: does it fit the session length and elicit the decision-relevant information? Trim or resequence.

title: Analyze customer feedback, reviews, or survey comments
description: Finds themes, sentiment, and priorities in customer feedback, and what to do about them.
prompt:
Role: Act as a UX researcher analysing voice-of-customer feedback at scale.

Context: Feedback sources and volume (reviews, support tickets, survey verbatims, NPS comments, sales notes): [SOURCES_VOLUME]. Time range: [TIME_RANGE]. Product areas to tag against: [PRODUCT_AREAS]. Segments to break down by: [SEGMENTS]. What decision this feeds: [DECISION].

Task: Produce: a coding scheme (themes / sub-themes tied to product areas); a themed summary with, per theme, the frequency, sentiment, an estimate of severity/impact, representative quotes, and the trend over the range; where themes differ by segment; and a prioritised list of recommended actions (fix / investigate / monitor) with the rationale.

Format: Sections: Coding scheme | Themed summary (table) | Segment differences | Recommended actions. ~500 words.

Verification: Give counts, not vague quantifiers ('many'); note where the sample is skewed (e.g. reviews over-represent extremes). Keep quotes verbatim and attributed to a source type.

Validation: Check the top theme against the raw feedback: does the count hold up and is the severity estimate reasonable, not inflated by a few loud voices? Adjust.

title: Write a design brief and user-flow specification
description: Defines the user goal, flow, states, and edge cases for a feature.
prompt:
Role: Act as a product designer scoping a design before visual work begins.

Context: Problem and the user's goal: [PROBLEM_GOAL]. Requirements / PRD reference: [REQUIREMENTS]. Users and context of use (device, environment, frequency): [USERS_CONTEXT]. Existing patterns / design system: [DESIGN_SYSTEM]. Constraints (technical, accessibility, content): [CONSTRAINTS]. Success looks like: [SUCCESS].

Task: Produce: a design brief - the problem, the user and their goal, success criteria, principles to hold, and what is out of scope; then a user-flow spec - the happy path step by step, each step's purpose, the states (empty / loading / error / success), the edge and error cases and how they are handled, the content/microcopy needed, and the accessibility considerations per step.

Format: Sections: Design brief | User flow (numbered steps with states) | Edge & error cases | Content needs | Accessibility notes.

Verification: Flag any step whose purpose is unclear, any state not accounted for, and any place the flow assumes data or a permission that may not exist.

Validation: Walk a first-time user and an error-prone user through the flow: do both reach success without a dead end? Fix the step that fails them.

title: Assess technical feasibility and dependencies
description: Evaluates whether and how a feature can be built, plus its risks and dependencies.
prompt:
Role: Act as a technical product manager assessing feasibility with engineering input.

Context: The capability proposed and the user outcome: [CAPABILITY_OUTCOME]. Current architecture and relevant systems: [ARCHITECTURE]. Non-functional needs (scale, latency, reliability, security, compliance): [NFRS]. Timeframe and team capacity: [TIMEFRAME_CAPACITY]. Known technical constraints and debt in the area: [CONSTRAINTS_DEBT]. Third parties / platform limits involved: [THIRD_PARTIES].

Goal: Give the product and engineering leads an honest read on feasibility, the main options and what has to be true for it to land in the timeframe.

Task: Produce: (1) 2-3 implementation approaches at a high level, each with rough effort, the NFRs it would meet or strain, and its main technical risk; (2) the dependencies (internal teams, platform work, third parties, data) and their lead times; (3) the unknowns that most affect the estimate and a spike to resolve each; (4) a feasibility verdict for the timeframe (feasible / feasible with scope cut / not feasible) with the reasoning; (5) what scope could be cut to fit.

Constraints: Estimates are ranges with stated assumptions, not points. Do not claim feasibility without naming the dependencies and unknowns that could break it. Flag anything needing a security or compliance review. Be explicit where engineering input is required to firm up the estimate.

Examples: Approach row: 'Approach | Rough effort | NFRs met/strained | Main risk | Key dependency.' Unknown row: 'Unknown: can [system] sustain [X] writes/sec? Spike: load test a prototype, 2 days. Effect if no: approach A is off the table.'

Format: Sections: Approaches (table) | Dependencies & lead times | Unknowns & spikes | Feasibility verdict & reasoning | Scope-cut options. ~650 words.

Verification: List every assumption behind the effort ranges and every dependency without a confirmed lead time.

Validation: Pressure-test the verdict: if the two biggest unknowns resolve badly, is it still feasible? State the fallback and the decision point.

title: Set product vision, strategy, and OKRs
description: Vision, strategy, and outcome-based OKRs for a product or team.
prompt:
Role: Act as a head of product setting direction for a product line.

Context: Product and where it is today (traction, strengths, problems): [CURRENT_STATE]. Company strategy and constraints it imposes: [COMPANY_STRATEGY]. Market and customer trends: [TRENDS]. Target customers and the value we intend to create: [TARGET_VALUE]. Competitive context: [COMPETITION]. Time horizon for the vision and the OKR period: [HORIZONS]. Capacity: [CAPACITY].

Goal: Give the team a clear, motivating direction and a strategy with real choices, plus OKRs that measure outcomes and fit capacity.

Task: Produce: (1) a vision statement (the future state for the customer, 2-3 sentences); (2) a strategy narrative - the target customer, the value proposition, the 3-4 strategic choices (where to play / how to win / what we will NOT do), and why they fit the company strategy and the trends; (3) the strategic bets for the horizon; (4) OKRs for the next period - 2-3 objectives with 2-4 outcome-based key results each, with baselines and targets, that ladder to the strategy and fit capacity; (5) the leading risks to the strategy.

Constraints: The strategy must contain genuine choices and explicit non-goals, not a list of everything. Key results measure outcomes (customer or business), not output or activity. Targets must be grounded in a baseline. Keep the whole thing under ~900 words.

Examples: Choice shape: 'We will win mid-market by [X]; we will NOT chase enterprise this year because [Y].' KR shape: 'Increase [activation metric] from [baseline] to [target] by [date].'

Format: Sections: Vision | Strategy narrative (choices & non-goals) | Strategic bets | OKRs (table) | Risks to the strategy.

Verification: Check each key result is an outcome with a baseline and target; flag any that is really an output or a task, and any strategic choice that is not actually a choice.

Validation: Stress-test the strategy: could a competitor copy it in a quarter, and does it force real trade-offs? If it is safe and all-inclusive, sharpen the choices.

title: Write release notes and stakeholder updates
description: Clear release notes for users and internal teams.
prompt:
Role: Act as a product operations specialist writing release communications.

Context: Changes shipped this release (features, improvements, fixes, with the user-facing effect): [CHANGES]. Audiences: customers, plus internal teams: [AUDIENCES]. Anything requiring user action or with limitations: [ACTIONS_LIMITATIONS]. Tone and format norms: [NORMS]. Links / docs available: [LINKS].

Task: Produce: (1) customer-facing release notes grouped as New / Improved / Fixed, each item in plain benefit-first language with a doc link where relevant, and a clear call-out for anything needing action; (2) an internal update for support and sales - what changed, who it affects, likely questions, and what to tell customers.

Format: Two blocks: Release notes (New / Improved / Fixed) | Internal update.

title: Analyze product adoption, retention, and churn
description: Reads product usage data to explain adoption, retention, and churn drivers.
prompt:
Role: Act as a product manager reviewing product analytics for a feature or the whole product.

Context: Scope and period: [SCOPE_PERIOD]. Data available (activation funnel, feature adoption, retention/cohort curves, churn events, segment splits): [DATA]. Definitions (activated, retained, churned): [DEFINITIONS]. Recent changes that could confound: [CHANGES]. The question this feeds: [QUESTION].

Task: Produce: (1) the funnel and where the biggest drop-offs are, by segment; (2) the retention / cohort picture and how it is trending; (3) churn analysis - when users churn and the behaviours or attributes correlated with it (labelled as correlation, with strength); (4) the 3 most likely, actionable drivers and the evidence; (5) recommended actions (with the metric each targets) and what to instrument or test to confirm the drivers.

Format: Sections: Funnel & drop-offs | Retention / cohorts | Churn analysis | Likely drivers | Actions & what to confirm. ~500 words.

Verification: Distinguish correlation from causation everywhere; note confounds from the recent changes; give numbers and sample sizes, not adjectives.

Validation: Challenge the leading driver: is there a simpler explanation (seasonality, a release, a measurement change)? Rule it in or out before recommending spend.

title: Write a business case for an investment or initiative
description: Costs, benefits, NPV/payback, risks, and a recommendation for any initiative or purchase.
prompt:
Role: Act as a head of product writing a business case for an executive decision.

Context: The opportunity and why now: [OPPORTUNITY_WHY_NOW]. Target customer and problem, with evidence: [CUSTOMER_PROBLEM_EVIDENCE]. Proposed solution and how it differs: [SOLUTION_DIFF]. Market size / reachable demand and basis: [MARKET]. Business model and pricing hypothesis: [MODEL_PRICING]. Cost to build and run (rough, phased): [COSTS]. Key risks and alternatives incl. do-nothing: [RISKS_ALTS]. Decision criteria and timeframe: [CRITERIA_TIMEFRAME].

Goal: Give the executive team a clear, honest basis to fund, stage-gate or decline, with the uncertainty made explicit rather than hidden.

Task: Produce: an executive summary; the problem and evidence; the market opportunity and its basis; the solution and its differentiation; the business model with a simple unit-economics view and the assumptions; a phased cost and a rough return / payback range; risks with mitigations; the comparison to do-nothing and the main alternative; and a staged recommendation (e.g. fund a discovery phase with a kill criterion) tied to the decision criteria.

Constraints: Use only the evidence and figures provided or clearly-labelled assumptions. Present a range, not a single forecast. Recommend the smallest next commitment that reduces the biggest uncertainty (stage-gate), not a full build. Be explicit about what could kill the case.

Examples: Stage-gate shape: 'Phase 1 (discovery, [cost], [X] weeks): validate [riskiest assumption]. Proceed only if [measurable condition]; otherwise stop.'

Format: Sections: Executive summary | Problem & evidence | Market | Solution & differentiation | Model & unit economics | Costs & return range | Risks | Do-nothing & alternative | Staged recommendation. ~900 words.

Verification: Collect every assumption in one list and mark which the case is most sensitive to.

Validation: Review as a sceptical CFO and a rival PM: which assumption is the case really betting on, and is the first stage-gate cheap enough and sharp enough? Tighten it.

title: Write a project charter
description: Defines a project's purpose, scope, objectives, stakeholders, and success criteria.
prompt:
Role: Act as a project manager writing the charter for a newly approved project.

Context: Project purpose and the business need: [PURPOSE_NEED]. Sponsor and key stakeholders: [SPONSOR_STAKEHOLDERS]. Desired outcomes and how success is measured: [OUTCOMES_MEASURES]. Known scope and explicit out-of-scope: [SCOPE]. Budget, timeline and resource envelope: [ENVELOPE]. Assumptions, constraints and dependencies: [ACDS]. Major risks: [RISKS].

Task: Produce the charter: purpose and background; objectives and measurable success criteria; scope and out-of-scope; key deliverables and milestones; stakeholder list with roles and interest; governance (decision rights, meeting cadence, reporting); assumptions, constraints, dependencies; top risks with initial responses; and a light business case (cost, benefit, and the cost of not doing it).

Format: A charter with numbered sections and a milestone table. ~600 words.

Verification: Check every objective has a measure and every deliverable maps to an objective; flag assumptions that, if wrong, would change scope or budget.

Validation: Review as the sponsor: is it clear what will be delivered, by when, for how much, and how we will know it worked? Tighten anything ambiguous.

title: Create a project plan with a work breakdown and schedule
description: WBS, milestones, dependencies, resources, and a realistic timeline.
prompt:
Role: Act as a project manager building the WBS and schedule.

Context: Scope and deliverables: [SCOPE_DELIVERABLES]. Known constraints (fixed dates, resource availability, external dependencies): [CONSTRAINTS]. Team and skills available: [TEAM]. Estimating basis / any historical data: [ESTIMATING_BASIS]. Methodology (predictive / agile / hybrid): [METHODOLOGY]. Risk areas: [RISK_AREAS].

Task: Produce: (1) a WBS decomposing each deliverable to work-package level with a one-line definition of done for each; (2) rough effort and duration per work package with the estimating assumption; (3) the dependency map and the resulting phased schedule with milestones; (4) the critical path and the work packages with the least float; (5) where the schedule is most fragile and the buffer or fast-track options.

Format: Sections: WBS (indented, with DoD) | Estimates (table) | Dependencies & schedule (phases + milestones) | Critical path & low-float items | Schedule risks & options. ~550 words.

Verification: Flag every estimate that lacks a basis and every dependency without a confirmed date; note where the WBS may be incomplete.

Validation: Pressure-test the critical path: if the two riskiest work packages slip by 20%, what is the end-date impact and the earliest mitigation? State it.

title: Build a RAID log (risks, assumptions, issues, dependencies)
description: Captures and tracks the risks, assumptions, issues, and dependencies on a project.
prompt:
Role: Act as a project manager compiling and structuring a RAID log.

Context: Project context: [PROJECT_CONTEXT]. Raw notes / status inputs mentioning risks, assumptions, issues, dependencies: [NOTES]. Scoring scale for risk (likelihood x impact): [RISK_SCALE]. Escalation thresholds: [ESCALATION]. Review cadence: [CADENCE].

Task: Produce: a categorised RAID log - Risks (description, cause, likelihood, impact, score, response strategy, owner, next action, date); Assumptions (statement, validity, what happens if false, owner); Issues (description, impact now, severity, owner, action, target date); Dependencies (what, on whom, needed-by date, status, owner). Then the items breaching escalation thresholds and a proposed agenda for the next RAID review.

Format: Four tables (Risks / Assumptions / Issues / Dependencies) + escalations + review agenda.

Verification: Do not invent items not implied by the notes; flag notes that are too vague to log and need clarification. Apply the risk scale consistently.

Validation: Check the log against the project's biggest known threat: is it captured with a real response and owner, or buried? Elevate it if so.

title: Write an executive project status report
description: A RAG status report: progress, risks, decisions needed, and next steps.
prompt:
Role: Act as a project manager writing the weekly executive status report.

Context: Reporting period: [PERIOD]. Overall status and the reason: [STATUS_REASON]. Progress vs plan (milestones hit / missed, % complete, budget vs plan): [PROGRESS]. Top risks and issues with current action: [RISKS_ISSUES]. Decisions or help needed from the sponsor: [ASKS]. Next period's focus: [NEXT].

Task: Write a one-page report: overall RAG with a one-line reason; progress vs plan (schedule, scope, budget); the 3 things going well; the 3 risks/issues that matter with the action and owner; the decisions or support needed; and next period's key activities.

Format: A one-page structured report (RAG | Progress | Going well | Watch list | Asks | Next). Under 300 words.

title: Create a risk register with mitigations
description: Identifies, scores, and plans responses to project or business risks.
prompt:
Role: Act as a delivery lead building and analysing the project risk register.

Context: Project scope, approach and phase: [SCOPE_PHASE]. Known risk sources (technical, resource, external, commercial, change, dependency): [RISK_SOURCES]. Risk scale and appetite: [SCALE_APPETITE]. Schedule and budget baselines: [BASELINES]. Contingency available (time / budget): [CONTINGENCY]. Lessons from similar projects: [LESSONS].

Goal: Give the project board a clear view of the risk exposure and a credible plan to keep it within appetite.

Task: Produce: (1) the risk register - each risk with cause, trigger, likelihood, impact (schedule/cost/quality), score, and proximity; (2) a response per risk (avoid / reduce / transfer / accept) with the specific actions, owner and cost; (3) contingency plans for the top risks with the trigger that activates them and the reserve they draw on; (4) the overall exposure vs contingency and whether it is within appetite; (5) the 5 risks to review weekly.

Constraints: Score consistently on the given scale; base likelihood on evidence or the lessons, not optimism. Contingency plans must name a concrete trigger, not 'if things go wrong'. Make clear where residual risk still exceeds appetite.

Examples: Register row: 'Risk: key integration partner delivers late. Cause: their competing priorities. Trigger: no API spec by [date]. L: high, I: 3-wk slip. Response: reduce - weekly joint checkpoint + parallel stub build. Owner: [name]. Contingency: if trigger hits, activate stub (draws 2 wks reserve).'

Format: Sections: Risk register (table) | Responses & costs | Contingency plans (trigger -> action -> reserve) | Exposure vs contingency | Weekly-review list. ~700 words.

Verification: Recompute total potential schedule/cost exposure of the un-mitigated top risks and compare to contingency; flag risks scored on assumption alone.

Validation: Stress-test as a sceptical project board: if the top two risks both materialise, does the contingency actually cover it? State the honest answer and the pre-emptive move.

title: Assess the impact of a change request
description: Evaluates a scope change's impact on time, cost, quality, and risk.
prompt:
Role: Act as a delivery lead assessing a change request for the change control board.

Context: The change requested and who raised it: [CHANGE_REQUEST]. Reason / driver: [DRIVER]. Current baselines (scope, schedule, cost, quality): [BASELINES]. Current status and critical path: [STATUS_CP]. Dependencies and other in-flight changes: [DEPENDENCIES]. Benefits case it affects: [BENEFITS_CASE].

Task: Produce: a clear statement of the change and its rationale; the impact on scope, schedule (including critical path), cost, resources, risk, and the benefits case if accepted; the impact of NOT making the change; 2-3 options (accept as-is / accept modified / defer / reject) with pros, cons and cost; a recommendation with the reasoning; and the approvals needed.

Format: Sections: Change & rationale | Impact analysis (scope / schedule / cost / risk / benefits) | Do-nothing impact | Options | Recommendation | Approvals. ~450 words.

Verification: Quantify schedule and cost impact against the baselines and show the assumption; flag any impact you cannot size without more input.

Validation: Challenge as a sponsor watching the budget: is the recommendation driven by benefit and risk, or by avoiding a hard conversation? Re-justify if needed.

title: Plan stakeholder communication and engagement
description: Who needs to know what, when, and how — and how to keep them engaged.
prompt:
Role: Act as a programme manager building a stakeholder engagement plan.

Context: Programme purpose and change involved: [PURPOSE_CHANGE]. Stakeholders / groups and what we know about their interest, influence and current stance: [STAKEHOLDERS]. Key messages and any sensitivities: [MESSAGES_SENSITIVITIES]. Channels available: [CHANNELS]. Milestones that need communication: [MILESTONES]. Constraints: [CONSTRAINTS].

Task: Produce: (1) a stakeholder map (influence x interest) with the current and target stance for each and the gap; (2) an engagement approach per stakeholder/group (inform / consult / involve / collaborate) with the rationale; (3) a communication plan - message, audience, channel, sender, timing/cadence, and the feedback loop; (4) the risky stakeholders and a specific plan to move them; (5) how you will measure engagement.

Format: Sections: Stakeholder map (table) | Engagement approach | Communication plan (table) | At-risk stakeholders & plan | Engagement measures. ~500 words.

Verification: Flag any stance assessment that is an assumption rather than evidenced; ensure every milestone has a communication and every stakeholder a clear approach.

Validation: Pressure-test against the most resistant stakeholder: is the plan to shift them specific and realistic, or wishful? Sharpen it.

title: Plan a sprint or run a retrospective
description: Sprint goals and capacity planning, plus a retrospective format that leads to real change.
prompt:
Role: Act as a scrum master preparing to facilitate sprint planning and a retrospective.

Context: Team and its current situation (morale, recent delivery, any friction): [TEAM_SITUATION]. Sprint goal candidate and backlog readiness: [GOAL_BACKLOG]. Capacity and known absences: [CAPACITY]. Retro focus (what happened this sprint worth examining): [RETRO_FOCUS]. Anti-patterns you have seen in this team: [ANTI_PATTERNS]. Time available for each session: [TIMEBOXES].

Task: Produce: (1) a sprint planning facilitation plan - agenda with timeboxes, how to confirm/sharpen the sprint goal, how to right-size the commitment against capacity, and how to surface risks and dependencies; (2) a retrospective plan - a format suited to the focus and the team's state, the specific prompts, how to keep it psychologically safe, and how to land 3 concrete, owned improvement actions; (3) the facilitator moves for the anti-patterns you expect.

Format: Sections: Sprint planning plan (agenda + prompts) | Retrospective plan (format + prompts + safety) | Handling the anti-patterns.

Verification: Check the agendas fit the timeboxes; flag any part that would run long or that assumes backlog readiness you were not told exists.

Validation: Walk the retro plan against a team that had a bad sprint: would it stay constructive and produce real actions, or descend into blame? Adjust the risky step.

title: Prioritize projects in a portfolio
description: A scoring model to choose which projects to fund, pause, or stop.
prompt:
Role: Act as a portfolio manager prioritising the project portfolio against strategy and capacity.

Context: Strategic objectives and their relative weight: [OBJECTIVES_WEIGHTS]. Candidate and in-flight projects with value, cost, effort, risk, dependencies, and strategic fit: [PROJECTS]. Total capacity (budget and key resource types) per period: [CAPACITY]. Mandatory / compliance projects: [MANDATORY]. Balancing constraints (e.g. mix of run/grow/transform, risk appetite): [BALANCE_CONSTRAINTS].

Goal: Produce a funded, sequenced portfolio that maximises strategic value within capacity, with the logic transparent enough to defend to project sponsors.

Task: Produce: (1) the scoring model - criteria (strategic fit, value, risk, dependency, urgency), weights, and scoring guidance; (2) each project scored with the inputs shown and a confidence flag; (3) the ranked list, then the funded portfolio that fits capacity and honours mandatory projects and the balance constraints, with what is deferred and why; (4) the sequencing given dependencies and resource peaks; (5) the decisions where reasonable people would disagree, and the sensitivity to weight changes.

Constraints: Score only on the provided inputs; mandatory projects are in regardless but their capacity cost must be shown. The funded set must fit capacity and the balance constraints. Do not let project size or sponsor seniority drive rank. Make deferrals and their cost explicit.

Examples: Score row: 'Project | Strategic fit | Value | Risk (inv.) | Urgency | Weighted score | Confidence.' Deferral note: 'Deferring [P] costs ~[value] of expected benefit and slips [dependency]; revisit at [gate].'

Format: Sections: Scoring model | Scored projects (table) | Funded portfolio & deferrals | Sequence (dependencies + resource peaks) | Contested calls & weight sensitivity. ~750 words.

Verification: Recompute weighted scores for a sample; list projects whose rank flips under a plausible change to the objective weights.

Validation: Pressure-test as a sponsor whose project was deferred: is the call defensible on strategy and capacity, or is it an artefact of the weights? Re-examine if the latter.

title: Capture lessons learned from a project
description: A blameless lessons-learned write-up with actions for next time.
prompt:
Role: Act as a PMO analyst capturing lessons learned from a completed project or phase.

Context: Project summary and outcome vs plan: [PROJECT_SUMMARY]. Inputs (retro notes, review findings, RAID history, stakeholder feedback): [INPUTS]. The knowledge base structure and tags: [KB_STRUCTURE]. Audience who would reuse this: [AUDIENCE].

Task: Produce: 6-10 lessons, each as - situation, what happened, why (root cause), the impact, the recommendation for future projects, and the type of project/phase it applies to; group them (estimation, stakeholders, delivery, procurement, etc.); add the KB tags; and list the 3 lessons most worth turning into a checklist item or template change.

Format: Sections: Lessons (grouped, each with the 6 fields) | KB tags | Turn-into-standard candidates.

title: Assess my team's maturity and plan coaching
description: Evaluates how your team works today and where to focus coaching.
prompt:
Role: Act as an agile coach assessing a team and planning your coaching.

Context: Team context (composition, tenure, domain, delivery model): [TEAM_CONTEXT]. Observations and data (ceremonies, flow metrics, quality, stakeholder feedback, what you have seen): [OBSERVATIONS]. Maturity dimensions to assess: [DIMENSIONS] (e.g. delivery flow, technical practices, product/outcome focus, collaboration, continuous improvement). Constraints on your time and mandate: [CONSTRAINTS]. What 'better' would mean for this team: [GOAL_STATE].

Task: Produce: (1) a maturity rating per dimension (e.g. 1-5) with the specific evidence for each - not a vibe; (2) the 2-3 dimensions where improvement would most help delivery or outcomes, and why; (3) a 90-day coaching plan - the focus per fortnight, the interventions (workshops, pairing, facilitation, experiments), what the team will practise, and how you will know it is sticking; (4) the anti-patterns to watch for and how you will respond; (5) how you will reduce your involvement over time.

Format: Sections: Maturity assessment (table: dimension | rating | evidence) | Priority dimensions | 90-day coaching plan | Anti-patterns & responses | Fade-out plan. ~550 words.

Verification: Each rating must cite an observation or a metric; flag dimensions where you lack enough evidence and how you will gather it.

Validation: Test the plan against a team that is sceptical of coaching: is the first intervention low-friction and visibly useful? If not, change the opener.

title: Write an empathetic reply to a customer
description: Clear, warm, accurate responses to customer emails and chats.
prompt:
Role: Act as an experienced customer support agent for [PRODUCT].

Context: Customer message: [CUSTOMER_MESSAGE]. Account / context: [ACCOUNT_CONTEXT]. What we know about the issue and the correct resolution or next step: [RESOLUTION_FACTS]. Relevant policy / entitlement: [POLICY]. Tone and brand voice: [TONE]. What we cannot do or promise: [LIMITS].

Task: Write a reply that: opens by acknowledging the specific problem and its impact; gives the answer or the concrete next step in plain language; sets a clear expectation (what happens next, by when, what we need from them); and closes warmly. Match the brand voice and stay within policy and the stated limits.

Format: A ready-to-send reply. No internal jargon. Short paragraphs. One clear next step.

Verification: State only facts from the resolution notes and policy - do not invent capabilities, timelines, compensation or root cause. Flag anything the agent must confirm before sending.

Validation: Read it as the frustrated customer: does it show we understood, and is the next step unambiguous? Would it reduce or increase a follow-up contact? Tighten if it would increase one.

title: Summarize a support case for handover
description: A concise case summary so the next agent or team can pick it up without re-asking.
prompt:
Role: Act as a support agent writing internal handover notes for a colleague.

Context: Case thread / history: [CASE_HISTORY]. Who is picking it up and why (escalation, shift change, specialist): [HANDOVER_REASON]. Any commitments made to the customer: [COMMITMENTS]. Systems / references: [REFERENCES].

Task: Write internal notes: a one-paragraph situation summary; what has been tried and the result; the current state and any blockers; the agreed next step and any deadline or promise made to the customer; the customer's sentiment and sensitivity; and the key references (ticket IDs, logs, accounts).

Format: Sections: Situation | Done so far | Current state / blockers | Next step & commitments | Customer sentiment | References. Bullet points.

title: Design ticket categories and routing rules
description: A ticket taxonomy and routing rules that get issues to the right team fast.
prompt:
Role: Act as a support team lead standardising ticket categorisation and routing.

Context: Support teams / queues and what they handle: [TEAMS_QUEUES]. Current categories and their problems: [CURRENT_CATEGORIES]. Priority / SLA definitions: [PRIORITY_SLA]. Signals available (channel, product area, keywords, customer tier, sentiment): [SIGNALS]. Sample tickets with the correct handling: [SAMPLES].

Task: Produce: a category / subcategory scheme that is mutually exclusive and covers the samples; routing rules mapping category + signals to the owning queue; priority rules with a worked example per level; a rule for ambiguous or multi-issue tickets; and the sample tickets categorised, routed and prioritised to demonstrate it.

Format: Sections: Category scheme | Routing rules (table) | Priority rules | Ambiguous-ticket rule | Samples worked through.

Verification: Check the scheme has no overlapping categories and every sample maps cleanly; flag signals that are unreliable for routing.

Validation: Test with a multi-issue ticket and a vague one: does the scheme route them sensibly without a human guessing? Refine the fallback rule if not.

title: Create an escalation and human-handoff guide
description: When and how to escalate issues, or hand off from a bot to a human.
prompt:
Role: Act as a support team lead defining escalation and bot-to-human handoff rules.

Context: Channels and any automated/bot tier: [CHANNELS_BOT]. Escalation tiers and specialisms: [TIERS]. Situations that should always escalate (risk, VIP, legal, safety, repeated failure, high emotion): [ALWAYS_ESCALATE]. Situations that should stay in tier 1: [STAY_TIER1]. SLA and after-hours rules: [SLA_HOURS]. What context systems can pass: [CONTEXT_AVAILABLE].

Task: Produce: (1) the escalation triggers, each with the signal that identifies it and the destination tier/team; (2) the bot-to-human handoff triggers and how the handoff is done (what the customer sees, what context is passed, warm vs cold); (3) an anti-pattern list - when NOT to escalate; (4) the escalation note template (summary, what's been tried, why escalating, customer state, desired outcome); (5) 3 worked examples.

Format: Sections: Escalation triggers (table) | Handoff triggers & mechanics | Do-not-escalate | Escalation note template | Examples.

Verification: Ensure every 'always escalate' situation has a trigger and a destination; flag any trigger that relies on a signal the systems cannot actually detect.

Validation: Run a high-emotion but low-severity contact and a calm but high-risk one through the guide: does each go to the right place? Adjust the triggers that misfire.

title: Turn resolved tickets into a knowledge-base article
description: Help-center articles customers and agents can follow, built from real tickets.
prompt:
Role: Act as a knowledge base manager writing a customer-facing help article.

Context: The recurring issue and its ticket volume: [ISSUE_VOLUME]. Resolved ticket examples (symptom, cause, fix): [TICKET_EXAMPLES]. Product area and audience: [AREA_AUDIENCE]. Style guide and structure: [STYLE]. Related existing articles: [RELATED]. Known variations (by plan, platform, region): [VARIATIONS].

Task: Produce: a task-focused title; a one-line summary of what the article helps with; the symptoms it covers; the cause(s) in plain terms; numbered resolution steps (with the variation handled inline or in a sub-section); how to tell it worked; when and how to contact support if it did not; related links; and metadata (owner, review date, tags, search keywords).

Format: Sections: Title | Summary | Symptoms | Cause | Steps | Did it work? | Still stuck? | Related | Metadata.

Verification: Every step must trace to a resolved ticket pattern; do not generalise a one-off fix into standard advice. Flag variations not covered by the examples.

Validation: Test the article against one of the ticket examples not used to write it: would it have resolved that customer without contacting support? Fix the gap.

title: Write an FAQ page
description: FAQs built from real customer questions, with clear answers and logical grouping.
prompt:
Role: Act as a knowledge base manager writing an FAQ for a product area.

Context: Topic / feature: [TOPIC]. Real questions customers ask (from tickets, search, chat): [REAL_QUESTIONS]. The correct answers / source docs: [SOURCE_DOCS]. Audience and reading level: [AUDIENCE]. What is out of scope or sensitive: [OUT_OF_SCOPE].

Task: Produce 12-20 FAQs grouped by sub-topic. Phrase each question the way a customer would type it. Keep each answer to 1-3 sentences, accurate to the source docs, with a link to the fuller article where relevant. Flag any question that should route to a person rather than have a self-serve answer.

Format: Grouped FAQ list: Sub-topic > Q / A (with link). Plus a short 'route to support' list.

title: Recommend the next best action for a customer
description: Uses a customer's history to suggest the most helpful next step for the agent.
prompt:
Role: Act as a CX manager designing next-best-action guidance for agents.

Context: Customer signals available (product usage, tenure, tier, recent tickets, sentiment, lifecycle stage, entitlements): [SIGNALS]. Candidate actions (proactive tips, feature nudges, plan changes, retention offers, check-ins, escalations): [ACTIONS]. Business goals (retention, expansion, deflection, satisfaction) and their priority: [GOALS]. Guardrails (offer limits, do-not-contact, fairness, consent): [GUARDRAILS].

Task: Produce: (1) the signal set and how each is read; (2) for common customer situations, the recommended next best action and the reasoning, balanced across the goals; (3) the decision logic as clear rules or a decision table; (4) the guardrails as hard constraints the recommendation must never breach; (5) how an agent should present the action as a suggestion, not a script; (6) what to log to learn whether it worked.

Format: Sections: Signals | Situations -> recommended action & why | Decision table | Guardrails (hard rules) | Agent framing | Measurement.

Verification: Check no recommendation can breach a guardrail; flag situations where signals conflict and the logic is ambiguous.

Validation: Test on a churn-risk customer and a happy power user: are the actions genuinely helpful to the customer, not just to our metrics? Adjust anything that feels manipulative.

title: Build a QA scorecard for support conversations
description: A rubric to review and coach customer interactions consistently.
prompt:
Role: Act as a quality analyst designing the support QA scorecard.

Context: Channels covered: [CHANNELS]. What good service means here (resolution, accuracy, empathy, efficiency, compliance, brand): [QUALITY_DIMENSIONS]. Compliance / policy must-dos and hard fails: [COMPLIANCE]. How the score is used (coaching, not punitive; any thresholds): [USE]. Volume and who does reviews: [REVIEW_CONTEXT].

Task: Produce: (1) the scorecard - criteria grouped by dimension, each weighted, with a 3- or 4-point behavioural anchor (what earns each score, with an example); (2) auto-fail rules (compliance/safety breaches) and how they interact with the score; (3) a 'not applicable' rule; (4) calibration guidance so two reviewers score similarly, including 2 sample interactions scored; (5) how the results should feed coaching, not just a number.

Format: Sections: Scorecard (table: criterion | weight | anchors) | Auto-fail rules | N/A handling | Calibration guidance + 2 scored samples | Coaching use.

Verification: Flag anchors that are vague ('was empathetic') rather than behavioural; ensure the weights sum correctly and no criterion double-counts another.

Validation: Have two people score one sample with the anchors: do they land within one point? If not, tighten the anchor that caused the gap.

title: Write community responses and moderation guidelines
description: How to respond to and moderate an online community consistently and fairly.
prompt:
Role: Act as a community manager responding in a public forum and setting moderation guidance.

Context: The community post (content, tone, whether it is a complaint, question, feature request, or conflict): [POST]. Facts and our position on the issue: [FACTS_POSITION]. Community guidelines: [GUIDELINES]. Brand voice for public spaces: [VOICE]. What we cannot say publicly: [PUBLIC_LIMITS]. Escalation path for sensitive posts: [ESCALATION].

Task: Produce: (1) a public reply - acknowledge, give what we can say factually, set expectations, and move detailed or account-specific matters to a private channel; (2) whether and how to moderate (leave, respond only, edit, hide, lock, remove) against the guidelines, with the rationale; (3) reusable guidance for this category of post - the response pattern, the moderation decision tree, and when to escalate.

Format: Sections: Public reply | Moderation decision & rationale | Reusable guidance (pattern + decision tree + escalation).

Verification: Keep the public reply within the stated limits - no commitments, no internal detail, no naming individuals. Flag anything that should be legal-reviewed or escalated before posting.

Validation: Read the reply as other community members watching: does it look honest and calm, or defensive/corporate? Adjust. Would the moderation call look fair if screenshotted?

title: Create or rewrite support macros and templates
description: Consistent, on-tone response templates for common issues across channels.
prompt:
Role: Act as a support team lead improving the canned-response library.

Context: Current macros / templates (paste): [CURRENT_MACROS]. The problems with them (robotic, inconsistent, outdated, policy-wrong): [PROBLEMS]. Brand voice and tone principles: [VOICE]. Policy points that must remain exact: [POLICY_EXACT]. Channels and their constraints (chat length, email formality): [CHANNELS]. Personalisation fields available: [FIELDS].

Task: For each macro: rewrite it in the brand voice - warm, specific, no jargon - while keeping every policy statement exact; provide a chat variant and an email variant where the channel matters; use [placeholders] for personalisation and mark where the agent must add specifics; and add a one-line 'use when' note and a 'do not use when' note.

Format: Per macro: Use when | Do not use when | Chat variant | Email variant. Placeholders in [BRACKETS].

Verification: Diff each rewrite against the original policy content - flag any change in meaning. Ensure no macro is fully generic (each should still be tailored by the agent).

Validation: Read three rewritten macros back to back as a customer: do they sound like a person and consistent with each other? Fix any that still read as a form letter.

title: Clean a messy dataset
description: A step-by-step cleaning plan for duplicates, missing values, formats, and outliers.
prompt:
Role: Act as a data analyst assessing and preparing a business dataset.

Context: Dataset description and schema (columns, types, meaning, grain): [SCHEMA]. Sample rows or profile stats: [PROFILE]. Known issues: [KNOWN_ISSUES]. Intended analysis / use: [INTENDED_USE]. Business rules the data should obey: [BUSINESS_RULES]. Tools available: [TOOLS].

Task: Produce: (1) a data-quality assessment - completeness, validity, consistency, uniqueness, accuracy signals, and timeliness, each with what you found and its severity for the intended use; (2) a cleaning plan - each issue, the transformation to apply, the rule, and what could go wrong; (3) the validation checks to run after cleaning (row counts, distributions, referential integrity, business-rule checks); (4) the issues that need a data-owner decision rather than a technical fix.

Format: Sections: Data-quality assessment (table) | Cleaning plan (table: issue | transform | rule | risk) | Post-clean validation checks | Needs a data-owner decision. ~500 words.

Verification: Do not silently drop or impute without flagging the impact on the intended analysis; quantify how many rows each step affects. Flag assumptions about column meaning.

Validation: Check the plan against the intended analysis: would the cleaned dataset actually support it, or does a fix distort the metric that matters? Adjust.

title: Write a SQL query from plain English
description: Turns a business question into SQL, with validation checks and an explanation.
prompt:
Role: Act as a data analyst writing and validating SQL for a business question.

Context: The business question: [QUESTION]. Schema (tables, key columns, types, relationships, grain): [SCHEMA]. Metric and dimension definitions that apply: [DEFINITIONS]. Known data quirks (soft deletes, timezones, late-arriving data, duplicates): [QUIRKS]. SQL dialect: [DIALECT]. Row-count or spot-check figures I can compare against: [KNOWN_FIGURES].

Goal: Return a query that answers exactly the question asked, with the interpretation and assumptions explicit and a way to confirm the result is right.

Task: Produce: (1) a restatement of the question in precise terms, listing every interpretation choice (time grain, filters, how the metric is defined, how nulls and duplicates are handled); (2) the SQL, readable, with comments on the non-obvious parts; (3) validation steps - checks to run (row counts, totals, a spot-check against a known figure, an edge-case filter) and what each would reveal if wrong; (4) common ways this query could be subtly wrong and how you guarded against them.

Constraints: Use only tables/columns in the provided schema - do not assume columns exist. Handle the stated quirks explicitly. If the question is ambiguous, pick the most likely interpretation, state it, and note the alternative. Show the assumptions, do not bury them.

Examples: Interpretation note: '"Active users last month" = distinct user_id with >=1 event where event_date in the previous full calendar month, excluding is_internal=true and soft-deleted users (deleted_at is null).'

Format: Sections: Question restated + interpretation choices | SQL (commented) | Validation steps | Subtle-error risks & guards.
